findings.title: Installer identity check is skipped for new installations
findings.body: GitHubInstallation.dispatch returns pipeline.next_step() as soon as Integration.objects.get(external_id=installation_id) raises DoesNotExist (integration.py around line 481). That is the normal install path: assert_setup_flow never creates a webhook Integration and still finishes successfully. It is also the race where GitHub's setup redirect arrives before the installation webhook. build_integration only reads installation_id (and optional sender); it never reads github_authenticated_user, so the OAuth login collected by OAuthLoginView is discarded. Linking then uses the GitHub App's own credentials. Anyone who knows a Sentry GitHub App installation_id (it is in the post-install redirect and in GitHub's installation settings URL) can attach that installation to their Sentry organization before an Integration row exists. After that, the real installer hits the existing "installed on another Sentry organization" error and is locked out. The new sender comparison only runs later, and only when an ACTIVE Integration already exists and has no OrganizationIntegration.

findings.title: OAuth state is not unique per install attempt
findings.body: OAuthLoginView sets the OAuth state query parameter to pipeline.signature (integration.py line 402) and later accepts the callback when that value matches (line 412). The new tests require this state to be exactly 9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3 for every fresh pipeline, including organization_2's pipeline in test_github_installed_on_another_org, which only reaches the "installed on another Sentry organization" error after the state check. So the value is not a per-flow nonce. PipelineAdvancerView has csrf_protect = False and auth_required = False, and the callback is a GET, so a top-level navigation still sends the session cookie under SameSite=Lax. Any user can start an install, copy state from their own authorize redirect, and send a victim who has an in-progress pipeline to /extensions/github/setup/?code=<attacker code>&state=<that value>&installation_id=<attacker installation>. The callback is accepted, github_authenticated_user becomes the attacker, and the sender check then passes because both sides are the attacker, linking the attacker's GitHub App installation to the victim's Sentry organization.

findings.title: installation_id is stored before the callback is authenticated
findings.body: OAuthLoginView copies request.GET installation_id into pipeline state (integration.py lines 397-399) before it checks state or exchanges the code. A request that only has installation_id still performs that write and then redirects to GitHub OAuth because state is missing (line 401). GitHub's OAuth callback does not include installation_id, so it will not clear the poisoned value. GitHubInstallation also prefers a query-string installation_id over the saved one (lines 448-450). The setup endpoint is an unauthenticated GET with CSRF disabled, so a user who already has an install pipeline and opens .../extensions/github/setup/?installation_id=<id> gets that id attached to their session. After they complete the OAuth step, the pipeline links that substituted installation. Together with the branch that skips the installer check when no Integration row exists, a malicious link during install attaches the attacker's GitHub App installation to the victim's Sentry organization.

findings.title: Token exchange omits redirect_uri sent at authorize
findings.body: The authorize redirect always includes redirect_uri (integration.py lines 404-408), but the access-token POST (lines 416-423) sends only code, client_id, and client_secret. GitHub's token endpoint, and OAuth 2.0 RFC 6749 section 4.1.3, require the same redirect_uri on the token request when it was included in the authorization request; otherwise GitHub returns an error and no access_token. This code treats a missing access_token as a failed install and shows "Invalid installation request." The new tests stub https://github.com/login/oauth/access_token to always return a token, so they never observe the rejection. The authorize URL is also built with string interpolation instead of urlencode, so redirect_uri is not percent-encoded and can fail to match a properly encoded value. Because every GitHub install now goes through this step, token exchange can fail for all users once it is live.

findings.title: Installer check crashes when sender login is missing
findings.body: When an ACTIVE Integration exists but has no OrganizationIntegration, the code compares the OAuth login to integration.metadata["sender"]["login"] (integration.py lines 501-504) with no existence check. build_integration only writes metadata["sender"] if state already contains sender, and test_basic_flow expects a pipeline-created integration to have no sender key at all. Hitting this branch for a row without that nested login (pipeline-created integration, older webhook data, or sender stored as a string) raises KeyError or TypeError. The user gets a 500 instead of the installation-failed dialog, and the security comparison never runs. A missing sender should fail closed through error().

findings.title: New security checks are not actually asserted
findings.body: test_installation_not_found still stubs the installation API as 404, but the follow-up request uses state=ddd023d87a913d5226e2a882c4c4cc05, which is not the pipeline signature the other tests use (9cae5e88803f35ed7970fc131e6e65d3). OAuthLoginView rejects that state and returns the generic invalid-installation page before build_integration or the 404 path runs. The assertion was changed from "The GitHub installation could not be found." to "Invalid installation request.", so the test stays green if 404 handling is removed. test_github_user_mismatch has the same blind spot: it only asserts that generic string, which is also what state mismatch and token failure return, so it does not prove the sender comparison ran. That test also changes installation id and sender.login on INSTALLATION_EVENT_EXAMPLE but keeps the original X-Hub-Signature (test_integration.py line 423). If webhook signature verification is enabled, the webhook is rejected and no Integration with sender "attacker" is created, so the mismatch path is never set up.
